sections.text:
Zanati revera non e Perside sed ex Africana stirpe oriundus; qui inter geomantiae
auctores apud Arabes clarissimus fuit; cf. Steinschneider, Die hebräischen Ueber-
setzungen des Mittelalters, 1893, p. 855, § 528. Opus eius videtur ex Arabica lingua
in Persicam translatum esse (nisi Persae astrologo byzantino Arabes sint), e Per-
sica vero in Graecam illud vertit anno 1266 Arsenius monachus (cf. supra, cod.
Neap. 19, p. 31 ss.; cod. Bonon. 18, f. 296v et praeterea cod. Vindob. phil. gr. 108
[Nessel]. — Aliud excerptum eiusdem scriptoris ex cod. Neap. 19, f. 393 infra
edetur.
[F. C.]
sections.en: Zanati in truth originated not from Persia but from African lineage; who among the authors of geomancy was most famous among the Arabs; cf. Steinschneider, Die hebräischen Uebersetzungen des Mittelalters, 1893, p. 855, § 528. His work seems to have been translated from the Arabic language into Persian (unless to the Byzantine astrologer Persians are Arabs), and from Persian into Greek the monk Arsenius translated it in the year 1266 (cf. above, cod. Neap. 19, p. 31 ss.; cod. Bonon. 18, f. 296v and besides cod. Vindob. phil. gr. 108 [Nessel]. — Another excerpt of the same writer from cod. Neap. 19, f. 393 will be edited below. [F. C.]

summary.headline: Fatal Days and Zanati
summary.text: A prognostic passage states that bleeding, taking a remedy, or eating meat on certain days leads to death within specified periods, and that a child born then will die violently and be short-lived. A footnote identifies Zanati as an African-born geomancer whose work passed from Arabic through Persian into Greek via the monk Arsenius in 1266.
